raw_text:
# Cardiac Contractility Modulation Therapy for Heart Failure: A Narrative Review

## Introduction

Heart failure (HF) remains a major global health burden, affecting more than 64 million people worldwide and accounting for substantial morbidity, mortality, and healthcare expenditure [1]. Despite advances in guideline-directed medical therapy and device-based interventions such as cardiac resynchronization therapy (CRT), a large proportion of patients remain symptomatic [2]. Notably, CRT is only indicated in patients with a wide QRS complex, leaving the majority of HF patients with narrow QRS ineligible [3]. Cardiac contractility modulation (CCM) has emerged as a device-based therapy designed to improve contractility and symptoms in patients with heart failure with reduced ejection fraction (HFrEF), particularly those who do not qualify for CRT [4].

## Mechanism of Action

CCM therapy delivers non-excitatory electrical signals to the right ventricular septum during the absolute refractory period of the cardiac cycle [5]. Because these signals are timed to the refractory period, they do not initiate a new action potential but instead modulate myocardial contractility [6]. The proposed mechanisms involve enhancement of intracellular calcium handling, increased sarcoplasmic reticulum calcium uptake, and normalization of phosphorylation of key calcium-handling proteins such as phospholamban and the ryanodine receptor [7]. Experimental and molecular studies have demonstrated reversal of the fetal gene program and improvement in expression of genes encoding sarcoplasmic reticulum calcium ATPase (SERCA2a) [8]. Importantly, unlike inotropes, CCM appears to enhance contractility without a corresponding increase in myocardial oxygen consumption, suggesting a more favorable energetic profile [9].

## Clinical Evidence

The clinical development of CCM has spanned several randomized controlled trials. The early FIX-HF-4 study, a double-blind crossover trial, demonstrated improvements in peak oxygen consumption (peak VO2) and quality of life with CCM therapy [10]. The subsequent FIX-HF-5 trial evaluated patients with NYHA class III–IV symptoms and ejection fraction ≤35%; while the primary endpoint of ventilatory anaerobic threshold was not met, prespecified subgroup analyses suggested benefit in patients with ejection fraction between 25% and 45% [11]. This finding informed the design of the FIX-HF-5C study, which prospectively enrolled patients with ejection fraction between 25% and 45% and demonstrated significant improvements in peak VO2, quality of life measured by the Minnesota Living with Heart Failure Questionnaire, and NYHA functional class [12].

A pooled analysis of individual patient data from the randomized trials confirmed improvements in exercise tolerance and quality of life, with consistent benefits across subgroups [13]. Long-term observational data and registries have supported the durability of these benefits and suggested possible reductions in HF hospitalizations [14]. The CCM-REG registry reported sustained improvements in NYHA class and quality of life over up to 24 months of follow-up, along with better-than-predicted survival [15].

## Safety and Patient Selection

CCM, delivered via the Optimizer system, has demonstrated a favorable safety profile in clinical trials, with complication rates comparable to other implantable cardiac devices [16]. The therapy received CE mark approval in Europe and U.S. Food and Drug Administration approval in 2019 for symptomatic HFrEF patients with narrow QRS who remain symptomatic despite optimal medical therapy [17]. Current candidates are typically patients with NYHA class III symptoms, ejection fraction between 25% and 45%, QRS duration less than 130 ms, and who are not candidates for CRT [18]. Appropriate patient selection is critical, and emerging data are exploring its role in HF with preserved or mildly reduced ejection fraction [19].

## Emerging Applications and Future Directions

Recent investigations have examined CCM in broader populations, including patients with atrial fibrillation, those with higher ejection fractions, and combination with defibrillator therapy [20]. The newer-generation Optimizer Smart and Optimizer Integra CCM-D systems aim to integrate defibrillation capabilities, potentially reducing device burden [21]. Studies are also evaluating effects on biomarkers such as natriuretic peptides and on reverse remodeling assessed by echocardiography and cardiac magnetic resonance [22]. Ongoing trials, including studies in HF with preserved ejection fraction, will help define the expanding indications [23]. Cost-effectiveness analyses suggest that CCM may be economically reasonable in appropriately selected populations, although further data are needed [24].

## Conclusion

CCM represents an important addition to the device-based therapeutic armamentarium for HFrEF, particularly for the substantial population of symptomatic patients with narrow QRS who are ineligible for CRT [25]. The accumulated evidence demonstrates consistent improvements in exercise capacity, symptoms, and quality of life, with an acceptable safety profile [26]. While questions remain regarding effects on hard outcomes such as mortality, ongoing trials and registries continue to refine its role [27]. As understanding of its molecular mechanisms deepens [28] and device technology advances [29], CCM is poised to become an increasingly integral component of personalized heart failure management [30].
